finding.claim: Broken authorization on DELETE /files/<fid>: the import aliases the boolean predicate `is_allowed` as `require_allowed`, and its return value is discarded, so no check is enforced. Any caller, including unauthenticated ones, can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any or no user header, for an fid that exists in STORE

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed: the predicate is renamed to look like an enforcing function
f = STORE[fid] looked up from the URL parameter
require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") returns a bool that is ignored and never aborts
is_allowed only returns True/False; only ensure_allowed (acl.py:8) calls abort(403)

finding.guards_checked: No decorator, no before_request authorization (load_user only sets g.user), no check of the return value. rename_file correctly uses ensure_allowed, which confirms this is an omission.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user from a header; the require_allowed call (alias of the bool-returning is_allowed) has its result discarded
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 calls it as a bare statement without aborting, so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 runs for any caller, unlike rename_file's ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10) which aborts 403.

finding.claim: Identity is taken directly from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified with no signature, session or token validation. Any client can impersonate any user, including users holding grants, by setting the header. This is exploitable unless an upstream proxy strips and sets the header, which is not enforced in this code.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, fully attacker-controlled
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26, which authorizes the rename at views.py:27, and the grants lookup at acl.py:5

trace.note: g.user is passed to the ACL check
resource grants are keyed by the claimed username, so a spoofed name inherits that user's grants
f["name"] is overwritten with attacker-supplied JSON

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware, no HMAC or JWT verification, no check that the request came from a trusted proxy. Only 2 source files exist, so no external gateway config could be reviewed.

verdict.guard_found: none in this code. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 correctly, but it checks grants for the attacker-chosen g.user, so it does not block impersonation. No auth middleware, signature check or proxy trust check exists.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client header, and views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, which looks up grants by that name at acl.py:5, so an anonymous client can send a grant-holder's name and reach the rename at views.py:27; the only possible mitigation is an upstream proxy stripping the header, which can't be checked from this code.
